headline: Grateful for kind professors

headline: A good cry and a long ride
summary: After an evening of thinking about his father, Roosevelt lets himself break down and feels better for it. He rides twenty miles on his horse Lightfoot and writes Conie, who is in Philadelphia with their mother and Aunt Susan West.

events.detail: Diary entry on grieving for his father
Rides 20 miles on Lightfoot
Writes Conie
Mittie and Conie stay with Aunt Susan West

letters.topic: Letter to his sister while she is in Philadelphia

tr_quotes.text: Have been thinking about Father all evening, have had a good square breakdown, and feel much the better for it.

headline: Leaning on Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes that the loss is only now sinking in. He asks Bamie for her counsel, telling her she resembles their father more than anyone else in the family.

events.detail: Diary note that the loss is just beginning to register
Asks Bamie for advice and help now that Father is gone

letters.topic: Asks for her guidance; says she is most like their father

tr_quotes.text: It seems as if I could only begin to realize it now.
You will have to give me a great deal of advice and assistance, now that our dear father is gone, for in many ways you are more like him than any of the rest of the family.

headline: First glass ball shoot
summary: At the first meeting of a glass ball shooting club, Roosevelt breaks 11 of 25 targets. He forces himself to keep busy but cannot yet face socializing with classmates.

events.detail: Breaks 11 of 25 glass balls at the club's first meeting
Writes of keeping busy through his grief

tr_quotes.text: Had the first meeting of the glass ball club. I broke 11 out of 25.
It seems so brutal to go about my ordinary occupations, but I must keep employed. I can not bear to mix with the fellows yet.

headline: 'Thy will be done'
summary: Roosevelt admits to bitter moments and fears what too much idle time might do to him, yet finds he can accept his loss with humble faith.

events.detail: Diary entry on grief and faith

tr_quotes.text: Every now + then there are very bitter moments; if I had very much time to think I believe I should almost go crazy. But I think I can really and humbly say 'Thy will be done'.

headline: Dreaming of a life in science
summary: Measuring himself against his father, Roosevelt feels his own life is weak by comparison. He writes that he would like to become a scientist and will miss his father's advice.

events.detail: Diary entry on his ambitions and his father's example

tr_quotes.text: Looking back on his life, it seems as if mine must be such a weak useless one in comparison.
I should like to be a scientist; oh, how I shall miss his sweet, sympathetic advice!

headline: Eleven of 22 at the glass ball club
summary: At another Glass Ball Club meeting, Roosevelt hits 11 of 22 targets.

events.detail: Shoots 11 of 22 glass balls

tr_quotes.text: Shot 11 out of 22

headline: A month since his father died
summary: The lightweight wrestling matches he had trained for take place, but they feel distant now. Roosevelt marks one month since his father's death, the worst day he has known.

events.detail: The lightweight wrestling contest is held
Marks a month since his father's death

tr_quotes.text: The light weight wrestling occured today. It is funny to look back and remember how I had trained for and anticipated it. It seems as if it was years ago. It is just one month since the blackest day of my life.

headline: Comforting his mother by letter
summary: Roosevelt teaches Sunday school, then breaks down again thinking of his father. He writes Mittie a tender letter wishing he could be at her side.

events.detail: Teaches his Sunday school class
Diary entry on his memories of Father
Writes his mother to console her

letters.topic: Longs to be home to comfort her in their grief

tr_quotes.text: Have been thinking over the many, many lovely memories I have of him; had another square breakdown.
My own heart's darling, I have so longed to be with you
to try to comfort you during this, our season of sorrow.

headline: Busy enough not to brood
summary: Roosevelt counts himself lucky that a full schedule leaves little time for dwelling on his loss.

events.detail: Diary note on keeping busy

tr_quotes.text: It has been a most fortunate thing for me that I have had so much to do that I have not had much time to think.

headline: Letters from home, none to Father
summary: Roosevelt treasures the loving letters from his family and finds it strange no longer to write to his father.

events.detail: Diary reflection on letters from home

tr_quotes.text: It is really wonderful, what sweet, unselfish letters the dear ones at home send me. It seems so strange never to write to him.

headline: Father's letters as a talisman

events.detail: Rereads his father's letters

tr_quotes.text: Looked over his sweet, affectionate letters. They will always be to me a talisman against evil.

tr_quotes.text: Have been looking over my Egyptian journal: every incident is connected with him.
he shared all my joys, and in sharing doubled them. and soothed all the few sorrows I ever had. But it is worse for Mother and the girls than for me; I wish so that I could be with them now.

tr_quotes.text: It is as if part of myself had been taken away. Every event of my life is bound up with him: he was as pure and unselfish as he was wise and good. But I have very much left to be grateful for.

He was so fond of all amusements and outdoor sports, as riding, sailing and shooting; and without a particle of cant, was so deeply religious.

headline: Bruised by Bacon, bird club at night

headline: Longing for home, dreading it too
summary: Roosevelt can hardly wait to see his family yet fears walking into a house without his father. He writes that every happy family memory includes him.

events.detail: Diary entry anticipating his return home

tr_quotes.text: It will seem so utterly unnatural for him not to be there. I can hardly conceive of a home without his presence; in looking back to all my happy family memories he is associated with every one. No evening was ever complete if spent without him.
Sometimes when I fully realize my loss I feel as if I should go wild.

headline: Sizing up his Sunday school boys

tr_quotes.text: After all, it is merely selfish grief. I know this thoroughly; but it is very terrible sometimes.

the only one that asks me questions is Watson, who is also very good; Ward is very good but frightfully stupid; Blennerhasset just as good, but much brighter; Kinsey bad and bright; Phillipot bad and stupid, and much the worst case of all.

I have lost the only human being to whom I told everything, never failing to get loving advice and sweet sympathy in return. No one but my wife, if ever I marry, will ever be able to take his place. I so wonder who my wife will be!

summary: With the spring's hard work behind him, Roosevelt catches himself still imagining his father's pleasure at each success.

events.detail: Diary entry on finishing the term and missing his father

tr_quotes.text: Thank fortune, all the hard work for this spring is over.
Very often, when I have done well in something I find my self thinking 'How pleased Father will be!' It seems perfectly terrible sometimes to think of never seeing him again; I long for him so.

headline: Boston hospitality and summer invitations
summary: Roosevelt credits his Boston friends' hospitality with brightening college life. Jack Tebbetts invites him to Schooner Head for a month and Harry Shaw for a Sunday. With his club table disbanded, he now eats at Memorial Hall beside Gorham Peters.

events.detail: Invited by Jack Tebbetts to Schooner Head and by Harry Shaw for a weekend
Takes meals at Memorial Hall with Gorham Peters

tr_quotes.text: All of my Bostonian friends have been very hospitable and kind, and by so doing have added wonderfully to the enjoyment of my college course.

uncertain: Schooner Head is located on Mount Desert Island, Maine, by general knowledge; the diary says 'Schooners Head'.

headline: Quiet day at Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; the record notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Botany exam, then off for summer
summary: Roosevelt finishes his botany final and leaves Cambridge that evening, heading for Oyster Bay as the term ends.

events.detail: Annual exam in botany
Leaves Cambridge for New York and Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: In evening left Cambridge for New York

headline: Oyster Bay full of Father
summary: Roosevelt reaches Oyster Bay around noon and finds every corner of the house tied to memories of his father.

events.detail: Arrives at Oyster Bay
Diary entry on missing his father

tr_quotes.text: Coming back here has recalled Father very vividly and very sadly to me.
It is impossible to tell in words how terribly I miss him.

headline: Warblers, a ride and a cry for Father
summary: Roosevelt collects a parula warbler and a grasshopper sparrow in Fleets Woods and takes a fine ride on Lightfoot. Annie Murray is visiting Conie, the Gracies are in town, and his grief breaks through again.

events.detail: Collects bird specimens in Fleets Woods
Rides Lightfoot
Annie Murray visits Conie
The Gracies are at Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Had a splendid ride on Lightfoot.
Father Father how bitterly I miss you, mourn you, and long for you!

uncertain: The Latin names in the record are read as parula warbler and grasshopper sparrow.

headline: Varnishing his boat
summary: Roosevelt sands and varnishes his boat. He is grateful for his family's affection but wishes his mother and Bamie would stop quarreling.

events.detail: Sandpapers and varnishes his boat
Notes friction between Mittie and Bamie

tr_quotes.text: Spent the morning in sandpapering and varnishing my boat.
There comes a dull pain at my heart whenever I think of the dear lost one.

headline: Seeing Father in the pew
summary: Four months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the sermon picturing him in his familiar corner of the family pew.

events.detail: Attends church, thinking of his father

tr_quotes.text: All through the sermon I was thinking of Father.
Oh, I feel so sad when I think of the word 'never'.

headline: Dawn tramp, then a boathouse
summary: Roosevelt is up with the sun for a long hike, back by nine, and spends the rest of the day building his boathouse.

events.detail: Long early-morning hike
Builds a boathouse

tr_quotes.text: Made a long tramp in the morning, rising with the sun and coming back at nine. Then built my boat house for the rest of the day

uncertain: The record does not mark this as diary; it is treated as TR's diary.

headline: Rainy day of chores, a petted son
summary: On a wet day Roosevelt divides his time among the boathouse, his gun and his rowboat, and worries that his doting family will spoil him.

events.detail: Works on boathouse, gun and rowboat

tr_quotes.text: I am afraid if I should stay long at home I should get spoiled and conceited, the family pet me up so.

headline: Riding with Annie Murray
summary: Roosevelt and Annie Murray ride out to Syosset and back through Laurel Hollow, then takes her rowing. He finds her sweet, pretty and clever; she leaves the next day.

events.detail: Horseback outing to Syosset and Laurel Hollow with Annie Murray
Takes her out in the rowboat

tr_quotes.text: She goes away tomorrow.

headline: Pine Island and the season's first swim
summary: Roosevelt rows to Pine Island, collects a pine warbler and takes his first swim of the year. He notes that all the Roosevelt young men but him are now in business.

events.detail: Collects a warbler on Pine Island
First swim of the summer
Observes his cousins and brother have gone into business

tr_quotes.text: Had my first swim.
This is the first summer that all the Roosevelt boys (except myself) have been in business.

uncertain: A species name is hard to read in the record; it is read as the pine warbler.

headline: Fanny Smith arrives; West smitten
summary: Fanny Smith has come to visit, and cousin West Roosevelt, who has loved her for three years, comes for tea. Roosevelt rows her to Cooper Bluff, where they race down the slope like children.

events.detail: Fanny Smith visits
West Roosevelt comes to tea
Rows Fanny to Cooper Bluff

tr_quotes.text: Poor fellow! He is really deeply in love with her and has been so for three years.

uncertain: A line about building the boathouse is crossed out in the original diary and is not used.

headline: Picnic at Yellow Banks
summary: Roosevelt picnics at Yellow Banks with Fanny, Conie and West, and in the afternoon takes Fanny on a long ride. The Gracies arrive for a stay of several weeks.

events.detail: Picnic at Yellow Banks
Long ride with Fanny Smith
The Gracies come to stay

tr_quotes.text: I like her very much.

headline: A gloomy stop at West 57th
summary: After church Roosevelt sets out for Harvard to take his last two exams, stopping for tea at the family's New York house, which feels empty and desolate.

events.detail: Morning church
Heads back to Harvard by way of New York
Tea at the empty family house

tr_quotes.text: The house was very gloomy and desolate, and thinking of Father made me feel so sad and lonely.

headline: Asthma sank his French exam
summary: After a botany exam, Roosevelt explains that he did badly on French three weeks earlier because asthma kept him awake the night before. He shrugs it off.

events.detail: Botany examination
Recalls an asthma attack that ruined his French exam

tr_quotes.text: It was terribly hard luck; thank heavens I am not of a nature to take things hardly.

headline: Elected to the A.D. Club
summary: After his final German exam, Roosevelt is surprised to be elected to the A.D. Club. He judges his second Harvard year happy and useful, and boards the night boat for New York.

events.detail: Final German exam
Elected to the A.D. Club
Takes the night boat to New York

tr_quotes.text: Funnily enough I was elected into the A.D. club - a totally unexpected social success.
I took the night boat to New York.

uncertain: One line is hard to read in the record and is not quoted.

headline: Remembering Father's nights of care
summary: Roosevelt visits Cassin in New York before going out to Oyster Bay. He recalls his father pacing the floor for hours carrying him through childhood asthma attacks.

events.detail: Visits Cassin
Goes out to Oyster Bay
Diary memory of his father's care during his asthma

tr_quotes.text: he did everything for me, and I nothing for him.

uncertain: Parts of this entry are hard to read in the record, so only a clear passage is quoted.

headline: Bad shooting, rowing and riding
summary: Roosevelt shoots poorly with the rifle, rows to Plum Point and goes riding.

events.detail: Rifle practice with poor scores
Rows to Plum Point
Horseback ride

tr_quotes.text: Made hideous scores with the rifle in the morning

headline: A happy outdoor summer
summary: Roosevelt describes his days of riding, tramping after specimens and rowing or sailing, gun in hand. He resolves not to be gloomy, since his father was always cheerful, and gallops twenty miles on Lightfoot.

events.detail: Diary entry on his outdoor life and outlook
Twenty-mile ride on Lightfoot

tr_quotes.text: Am leading the most intensely happy + healthy, out of doors life.
Father was himself so invariably cheerful that I feel it would be wrong for me to be gloomy.
Had a glorious 20-mile ride on Lightfoot; cantering the whole time.

headline: Sailing to Lloyd Neck with Alfred
summary: Roosevelt rows to Plum Point and back, then sails with Alfred to Lloyd Neck for lunch and some shooting. In the afternoon he rides with two girls; the day's bag is two herons and two sandsnipe.

events.detail: Rows to Plum Point
Sails with Alfred to Lloyd Neck to picnic and shoot
Afternoon ride

uncertain: Alfred is presumably cousin Alfred Roosevelt; 'the two girls' are not named. Diary spells it 'Loyds Neck'.

headline: Quiet Sunday at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A chickadee nest and a sunburn
summary: Roosevelt finds a chickadee nest on Pine Island and takes Nellie Beekman riding. His sunburned face, he jokes, looks like an undercooked lobster, and he frets about Elliott's friends.

events.detail: Finds a chickadee nest
Rides with Nellie Beekman
Worries about Elliott's companions

tr_quotes.text: My face is beginning. to look like an underdone lobster.

uncertain: The record identifies 'Chuff' as Ellie (Elliott).

headline: Rough water around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt rows around Centre Island in two hours, shooting along the way and taking on water in a heavy sea. A long gallop on the flat Long Island roads follows; he bags two sandpipers.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island in rough water
Shoots two sandpipers
Long ride

tr_quotes.text: There was quite a sea running and I shipped a good deal of water.

headline: Water lilies and a supper sail
summary: Roosevelt rides to Brookville and Glen Cove, walks Fleets Woods with his mother, drives Conie to Cold Spring for water lilies, rows to the marsh, and sails with Elliott at dusk, eating dinner aboard.

events.detail: Rides to Brookville and Glen Cove
Walks in Fleets Woods with Mittie
Drives Conie to Cold Spring to gather water lilies
Rows to the marsh
Evening sail and dinner aboard with Elliott

tr_quotes.text: Rowed to the marsh.

uncertain: Diary calls Mittie 'Muffie', Conie 'Pussie' and Elliott 'Chuffie'.

headline: At New London for the boat race
summary: Roosevelt travels to New London for the Harvard-Yale race, staying at Harry Chapin's with Minot Weld and Jackson.

events.detail: Goes to New London for the race
Stays at Harry Chapin's with Minot Weld and Jackson

tr_quotes.text: Came on here to see the race.

uncertain: The opponent in the race is not named in the entry; Jackson is named by surname only.

headline: Harvard wins; hoarse from cheering
summary: Harvard wins the race handily and Roosevelt shouts himself hoarse. He takes the night boat to New York that evening.

events.detail: Cheers Harvard to an easy victory
Takes the night boat to New York

tr_quotes.text: Harvard won easily. Am perfectly hoarse from shouting.

headline: A new Sharps rifle
summary: Back at Oyster Bay, Roosevelt buys a Sharps rifle, and Harvard takes the baseball championship.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay
Buys a Sharps rifle
Harvard wins the baseball championship

tr_quotes.text: Bought a Sharps rifle. Harvard won the baseball championship.

headline: 'Rest in trouble, not from trouble'
summary: A sermon line strikes Roosevelt, who credits his faith with carrying him through his grief; the family spends the evening singing hymns. Meanwhile President Hayes removes Chester A. Arthur and puts Edwin A. Merritt in charge of New York's customhouse.

events.detail: Hears a sermon and sings hymns with the family
Hayes removes Arthur and appoints Merritt as Collector

tr_quotes.text: I was much struck with one remark, that Christianity gives us, on this earth, rest in trouble, not from trouble. Nothing but my faith in the Lord Jesus Christ could have carried me through this, my terrible time of trial and sorrow.

uncertain: The record gives his name as Edwin Merritt.
